look: Brick terraces and grand stone streets like Regent Street, built in the 1810s and 1820s. For the Great Exhibition a giant hall of iron and glass, the Crystal Palace, went up in Hyde Park in a few months.
Men in dark frock coats and tall top hats. Women in wide, bell-shaped skirts over layers of petticoats, with shawls and bonnets. Poor workers wore patched coats and caps.
Horse buses, two-wheeled hansom cabs, carts and a lot of walking. Railways had spread across Britain in the 1840s; the first Underground line opened only in 1863.
Gas lamps on the main streets. At home people used candles and oil lamps.
Sellers everywhere: coffee stalls, pie men, flower girls. With about 2.3 million people, London was the biggest city in the world.

stops.name: Regent Street
stops.title: Regent Street, looking towards the Duke of York Column
stops.note: Half of a stereo photograph. Its museum dates it only roughly, so it may be some years after 1851.

spots.d: A tall column in memory of a son of King George III, finished in 1834.
spots.how: It still stands at the end of Waterloo Place.

spots.d: Regent Street was planned by the architect John Nash as a smart street of shops with columns and stone fronts.
spots.how: Most of these buildings were replaced in the 1920s, so photographs are how we know them.

spots.d: A light two-wheeled cab. The driver sat high up at the back, and the passenger rode in front, out of the mud.
spots.how: Joseph Hansom patented the design in 1834.

spots.d: Lamp posts burned coal gas piped under the street, and lamplighters lit them every evening.
spots.how: London's streets had been lit by gas since the 1810s.

stops.name: A coffee stall before dawn
stops.made: Printed in 1851, copied from a photograph
stops.title: The London Coffee-stall
stops.note: An engraving from Henry Mayhew's book London Labour and the London Poor. Photographs could not yet be printed in books, so an engraver copied one by hand.

spots.d: Before dawn, coffee stalls served workers on their way to work: a cup of coffee and a slice of bread for a penny or two.
spots.how: Mayhew interviewed coffee-stall keepers for his 1851 book about London's street people.

spots.d: Even working men wore top hats, often old and second-hand.
spots.how: You can see top hats on rich and poor alike in London pictures of the 1850s.

spots.d: Working women wrapped up in a big wool shawl, with a bonnet tied under the chin.
spots.how: The engraving was copied from a real photograph.

spots.d: The words under the picture say it was copied from a daguerreotype, an early kind of photograph, made by Richard Beard.
spots.how: Beard opened London's first photography studio in 1841.

stops.name: The Crystal Palace in Hyde Park
stops.title: The Great Exhibition building, north-west corner

spots.d: The Crystal Palace was put together from mass-made iron parts and about 300,000 panes of glass, in around five months.
spots.how: It was designed by Joseph Paxton, who had built giant greenhouses.

spots.d: Flags for the countries that sent their inventions, machines and art. More than six million visits were counted.
spots.how: The official records of the Exhibition.

spots.d: This picture was taken by William Henry Fox Talbot, one of the inventors of photography.
spots.how: Talbot announced his way of making photographs on paper in 1839.

stops.name: Opening day, 1 May 1851
stops.title: The opening of the Great Exhibition, 1 May 1851
stops.note: A watercolour by an artist who drew the event, so the colours are his.

spots.d: Queen Victoria and Prince Albert opened the Great Exhibition. Albert had helped to plan it.
spots.how: Victoria wrote in her diary that it was one of the greatest and most glorious days of their lives.

spots.d: A fountain made of pink and clear glass, about 8 metres high, stood at the centre of the hall.
spots.how: It was made by the glassmakers F. and C. Osler of Birmingham.

spots.d: The hall was built right over full-grown elm trees in Hyde Park, so they stood inside the glass.
spots.how: That is why the middle of the building had a tall curved roof.

spots.d: Women in their best: bonnets, shawls and huge skirts. Men in dark coats.
spots.how: The painter was there to record the day.
